news.title: Treasury Secretary Bessent says US entering 'endgame' with Iran, will sever economic lifelines
news.text: "At dawn begins an economic D-Day [against Iran], the single greatest financial offensive ever marshalled against an adversary," US Treasury Secretary Scott Bessent wrote in an opinion piece in the Financial Times on Sunday, echoing US President Donald Trump's statements on Truth Social last week."Our objective is to sever every economic lifeline that sustains the tyrannical regime until Tehran stands alone," he added.The US military has "significantly dismantled Iran's military capabilities and weakened its nuclear programme. Now we are entering endgame," Bessent wrote."President Trump has decimated Iran's economy to a point where the rial has never been weaker and inflation has rarely been higher," Bessent said in the FT, "The regime's final refuge now lies in the self-deception of fearful nations that still believe accommodating aggression can secure a durable peace.""Those who sever Iran's remaining financial and commercial connectivity will reinvigorate their own. They will deepen their access to global capital, reinforce confidence in their markets and attain the standing they seek in the world economy."The treasury secretary added that continued economic support will have negative consequences, saying "any nation that serves as a financial artery of a withering regime should expect to share in its isolation.""Those who fear the danger of defying Tehran ought not to discount the cost of testing Washington," he said, "Any remaining tie to Tehran will hasten the economic ostracism of countries and entities, whether that tie be purposefully constructed or wilfully ignored."The FT piece follows an interview Bessent gave to CNBC, and a series of statements from Trump which were posted to Truth Social about economic sanctions on Iran.Bessent said US would 'squash' Iranian economy"We are going to collapse this [the Iranian] regime," Bessent told CNBC on August 20. "You are either with us or against us - we are going to squash the economy of this murderous regime."Bessent explained that the US will be increasing economic pressure pressure on Iran, adding that if any of American allies continue doing business with Iran, whether transferring money, or buying their oil, "then the US Treasury and the US government, they will put its full might and force toward enforcing against you.""I see lots of reports that said, 'oh, well, this has never worked.' It does work, because we have a combination. It is a one-two punch," Bessent told CNBC. "We have the blockade, and we are going to have the toughest sanctions in history. And I will tell you, this will work. It worked in Venezuela once we put up the blockade. It is working in Cuba right now. And it is going to work in Iran, and we are going to collapse this regime.""This is going to be the greatest coordinated economic isolation in the history of the world."Statements from Trump about economic sanctions on IranTrump warned on August 19 that there would be significant economic consequences for any country that provided "any type of lifeline to Iran."In a post on Truth Social, Trump said Iran would face "Economic Warfare and Isolation on an unprecedented scale.""ANY country that allows its financial institutions, businesses, airports, or government entities to provide any type of lifeline to Iran will itself face TREMENDOUS Economic Consequences," Trump wrote.The president also announced that the US would enact "an ECONOMIC D-DAY" against Iran.
news.author: Esther Davis

news.title: Greece moves Patriot interceptor to protect key military base amid rising US-Iran tensions - report
news.text: Greece has moved a Patriot air defense battery to Crete following threats by senior Iranian officials against US bases in Europe, Greek newspaper Kathimerini reported on Sunday.The battery, personnel and equptment were moved overnight and are expected to be deployed near the Souda military base. Greece's Defense Ministry and armed forces remain on heightened alert as officials assess the potential threat to critical infrastructure and military facilities as tensions rise with Iran, Kathimerini added.The report explained that allied intelligence was concerned that Iran still has a significant number of ballistic missiles, with a reported range of over 2,000 km which would place parts of southeastern Europe, including Greece, within range.The Patriot defense system was deployed in March to protect against ballistic missile threats. Kathimerini added that Athens is in contact with the US and Israel over potential threats to military bases in Greece and Cyprus.Tehran considering attacking US bases in Europe if conflict escalatesSources close to the regime in Tehran warned that Iran may attack US military targets in Europe if US President Donald Trump escalated the conflict.The Financial Times reported that Tehran was seriously examining the options available to it to raise the stakes in the conflict, with many at the top of the regime seeing the renewal of the full-scale military confrontation as only a matter of timeTwo sources familiar with the details told the Financial Times that Iranian forces already conducted situational assessments regarding the possibility of attacking American assets in southeastern European countries.A prominent example of this is Bulgaria, which only last month approved the use of the Bessemer air base for US military refueling aircraft. Another source added that Cyprus, where a British air base was attacked by a drone last March, is also on the list of potential targets for retaliatory action in the event of a renewed American attack

news.title: 'Entering the endgame': US Treasury Secy Bessent says "economic D-Day" begins against Iran
news.text:
ANIThe US has vowed an unprecedented economic offensive to isolate Iran, while Tehran has threatened to halt Gulf oil exports and treat countries backing Washington’s campaign as acts of war. (In photo: US Treasury Secy Scott Bessent )

Washington: US Treasury Secretary Scott Bessent on Sunday (local time) said that the Trump administration is entering the "endgame" in its campaign against Iran, announcing what he called an "economic D-Day" aimed at severing Iran's economic lifelines.In a post on X, Bessent said, "President Trump has dismantled Iran's military capabilities, destroyed nearly 100 percent of its military factories, and buried its nuclear program."Also read: Trump’s economic isolation plan risks Iran strikes across Gulf— SecScottBessent (@SecScottBessent) "We are now entering the endgame. At dawn begins an economic D-Day -- the single greatest financial offensive ever marshaled against an adversary," he said.Bessent accused Iran of using security guarantees as a form of "extortion" and said Tehran had relied on the expectation that Iranian retaliation was certain while US enforcement could be negotiated.Live Events"The Islamic Republic has subsisted by dressing extortion as security guarantees. It has drawn strength from a calculus that regards Iranian retaliation as certain and American enforcement as negotiable," Bessent said."Under President Trump, that era is over. And those who fear the danger of defying Tehran ought not to discount the cost of testing Washington," he added.Bessent said Trump had created the conditions for the US government to deploy its full range of authorities against Iran."The President has created the conditions to leverage every agency, every authority and action many assumed we would never summon," he said."Our objective is to sever every economic lifeline that sustains the tyrannical regime until Tehran stands alone," Bessent added.Meanwhile, Iran's Supreme National Security Council Secretary Mohsen Rezaei on Monday warned that Tehran could halt all oil exports through the Strait of Hormuz and elsewhere in the Persian Gulf if the United States' "economic war" against Iran continues.Rezaei, in a post on X, also warned that Iran would consider any country supporting or participating in the US economic campaign against Tehran to be an "act of war.""If the economic war continues, not a single drop of oil will be exported. neither through the Strait of Hormuz nor from anywhere in the Persian Gulf. Iran will regard any country's participation in or support for America's economic war against the Iranian people as an act of war," Rezaei said.The warning comes amid heightened tensions between Tehran and Washington over US plans for tougher economic measures against Iran.Earlier on Sunday, Iranian Parliament Speaker Mohammad Bagher Ghalibaf ridiculed the United States following the fresh economic sanctions threat by President Donald Trump, using satirical commentary to argue that heavy-handed economic restrictions ultimately backfire.In a post on X, Ghalibaf commented on the limitations of trying to manage deep-seated financial strain through short-term state interventions and shared a sarcastic take on how economic pressures play out.Also read: Trump calls Strait of Hormuz ‘American territory’, warns Iran over nuclear arms"Importing frozen meat to fix meat prices. Okay, that might work. What's the plan for bonds, import frozen yields? Frozen homebuyers for housing? Frozen paychecks for wages? A frozen foreign policy delivers a frozen economy. The only thing still moving? The Iran boomerang," he said.Meanwhile, according to Al Jazeera, Iranian Foreign Ministry spokesperson Esmaeil Baghaei also slammed US' sanctions threat and said that war and sanctions are "not unfamiliar" to Iran.He noted that the Islamic Republic has been under sanctions for 20 years.Iran's rebuttal came after Trump on Wednesday announced what he called an "Economic D-Day" campaign against Iran, describing it as the "most crushing economic operation ever taken against any country."Trump said the campaign would amount to "Economic Warfare and Isolation on an unprecedented scale" and called on US allies to join Washington in isolating Iran.Trump also said Washington had "very draconian sanctions" available against Iran and indicated that additional measures could be announced."We have things that we could sanction. We have very draconian sanctions, and we'll see what happens," Trump said while addressing technology leaders.He said Washington would determine its next course of action based on developments, adding that the situation could either result in a significant fall in oil prices or lead to a continuation of the existing measures.On Thursday (local time), US Treasury Secretary Scott Bessent also warned Iran of the "toughest sanctions in history", saying Washington will pursue coordinated economic isolation against Tehran and seek to "collapse this regime", Al Jazeera reported.He urged US allies to join Washington in isolating Tehran, claiming that the measures would weaken Iran's ability to project influence globally.Bessent added that a media conference on Monday, i.e August 24, would reveal "exactly what we're going to do" against Iran.Add as a Reliable and Trusted News Source Add Now!

news.title: ‘Stop Nick Shirley Act’ is a disgraceful attack on the First Amendment
news.text:
The “Stop Nick Shirley Act” is California’s latest assault on the First Amendment.

Of course, Gavin Newsom, Mia Bonta, and the Democrats describe AB 2624 as a way to protect the “privacy” of “immigration support service providers.”

The media have largely played along, describing the bill as a way to protect immigrants.

But that’s not what the bill is, nor what motivated it.

The bill is an attempt to protect the non-profit organizations from scrutiny by journalists who are asking questions the state itself should be asking about potential fraud.

Citizen journalist Nick Shirley visited several sites in Minnesota and drew attention to fraud committed by organizations within the Somali community there. 

The problem was real, and well-known, but Minnesota Governor Tim Walz tried to cover it up, and accused critics of racism.

Shirley came to California to conduct more investigative journalism about mismanagement, grift, and fraud, just as The California Post has been doing.

That’s when Democrats in Sacramento decided to act.

AB 2624 would “prohibit a person, business, or association from soliciting, selling, or trading on the internet the personal information or image of a designated immigration support services provider, employee, or volunteer” with the intent of “that another person imminently use that information to commit a crime involving violence or a threat of violence.”

Inciting violence is already illegal. But AB 2624 suggests that if a journalist like Nick Shirley exposes fraud committed by an organization serving immigrants (which, in “sanctuary state” California, includes illegal immigrants), and someone else decides — illegally — to threaten that organization, then the journalist has committed a crime.

That is a violation of the First Amendment, and it will not stand up in court. It is just pandering to the amnesty lobby.

The California Post faces the same danger from this new law as citizen journalist like Nick Shirley does.

It aims to discourage reporting on non-profits — like our recent report on a non-profit CEO who is raking in millions.

Gavin Newsom styles himself as a defender of the First Amendment when he criticizes President Donald Trump, or Republicans who ban pornography from school libraries in other states.

But he has a track record of signing bills that violate free speech and are later struck down by the courts.

The most laughable example was in 2024, when he signed a law banning the use of AI in political ads.

That law was intended to protect Kamala Harris from mockery. It was tossed out the moment it hit a federal court.

And who could forget the prosecution of David Daleiden — later dropped — for the crime of undercover journalism exposing Planned Parenthood?

Journalists deserve protection, not intimidation. The “Stop Nick Shirley Act” is a disgrace.

news.title: From business leaders to sports fans, Canada responds to trade war escalation
news.text:
From business leaders to sports fans, Canada responds to trade war escalation

Canadians react to no deal

Prime Minister Mark Carney's decision to suspend trade talks with the United States has stirred up emotions on both sides of the border, and has drawn the ire of the U.S. president.

Early Sunday morning, Donald Trump took to his social media platform, Truth Social, in his first comments on the trade deal since negotiations fell apart late Friday night.

His post reignited his 51st state rhetoric, suggesting that "Canada wants the benefits of being a State, without being one!!!"

The post also said that Canada had, for too long, charged American farmers "massive amounts of Tariffs." A statement he punctuated with "No more!!! President DJT". He didn't expand on what tariffs he was referring to.

Like early on in the trade war, those taking in sporting events let Americans know how they felt. Canadian fans in Vancouver and Montreal booed the U.S. national anthem at the start of Major League Soccer matches on Saturday.

Buy Canadian talk was also ratcheted up. P.E.I. Premier Rob Lantz offered his support to Carney in a statement on Sunday, and asked residents to do their part.

"When you have the choice, buy local and buy Canadian," he said in the statement. "Every dollar spent on an Island or Canadian product supports the worker who made it, the farmer who grew it, the fisher who caught it, the producer who processed it and the business that put it on the shelf. Where we spend our hard-earned money matters. Those choices add up."

In a news release expressing support for the move, the Canadian Steel Producers Association said Canada and the U.S. have enjoyed more than 30 years of fully integrated trade and that "no deal is better than a bad deal."

In Brampton, Ont., mayor Patrick Brown echoed those words, saying more than 3,000 people remain out of work because of the shutdown of the Stellantis Assembly Plant, which was to be retooled for Jeep production before the company paused the plan in early 2025.

It then announced it was moving production of the Jeep Compass from Brampton to the U.S., and Brown says he's glad Canada's trade negotiators are holding firm.

"Prime Minister Carney and Minister (Dominic) Leblanc walked away from a bad deal instead of signing one that left our auto sector exposed, and Brampton knows better than almost anyone what's at stake if we get this wrong," Brown said in a news release.

The U.S. introduced new 50 per cent tariffs on billions of dollars' worth of Canadian exports on Saturday. The new U.S. tariffs target $28 billion in Canadian goods ranging from hockey sticks and honey to essential oils and dairy products.

Carney responded that retaliatory tariffs will hit the U.S. starting next month, starting Sept. 8, after Canada walked away from what he called a "bad deal." In a press conference on Saturday, Carney likened the negotiations to a war.

"We got attacked," Carney told reporters on Parliament Hill.

On Fox News on Sunday, the U.S Transportation Secretary Sean Duffy called Canada "a country that doesn't have a military" and said it was taking advantage of America.

"To think that they are going to go war with Donald Trump and actually win that war with the U.S., I think it's foolish on their part," Duffy said.

Canadian counter-levies will target sectors such as steel, dairy, appliances, agricultural equipment, pulp and paper, and electronics. Carney said more details on those retaliatory measures, as well as supports for affected sectors, will be announced in the coming days.

The Prime Minister's Office said Carney will announce new investments Monday "to defend our waters and strengthen our trade routes" along with Quebec Premier Christine Fréchette.

Not all leaders were cheering Carney's promise to match Washington's newest tariffs dollar-for-dollar, with Alberta Premier Danielle Smith noting retaliatory measures could mean Canadian farmers have to pay 50 per cent more for the equipment they need to produce our food.

Ontario Conservative MP Jamil Jivani, a longtime friend of U.S. Vice-President JD Vance, took to social media to call this a "solemn moment for hundreds of thousands" of Canadian families.

In audio from a fundraiser in Southampton, N.Y., on Wednesday, which was provided to The Canadian Press by a source who attended the private function, Vance praised Jivani for playing an active role in recent trade talks.

In response, former Alberta premier Jason Kenney criticized Jivani for not mentioning Trump's "constant, unprovoked attacks on our economy, and our sovereignty."

"But we are not cravenly surrendering in the face of constant economic and political aggression," Kenney said on social media.

Saskatchewan Premier Scott Moe, in a statement, said his government supports Carney's decision to enact dollar-for-dollar counter tariffs on targeted U.S. products. But he also noted it won't be easy, saying "all tariffs hurt real businesses and kill real jobs, on both sides of the border."

"That's why we should be doing everything we can to avoid, reduce and remove tariffs. I believe the federal government did that, but in the end, the U.S. administration chose to stick with this failed economic policy, and Canada must respond accordingly," Moe said.

Carney said that the U.S., "at the last hours," introduced efforts to restrict Canada's ability to have other trade deals. He called the move a "power play" that became an issue of sovereignty.

U.S. Trade Representative Jamieson Greer said Friday that the U.S. and Canada had "declined" to finalize a tentative agreement, and laid the blame entirely on Canada.

Some American politicians expressed disappointment in the Trump administration for the failed deal.

"Michiganders are uniquely impacted by DC Republicans’ ongoing, chaotic tariff wars with Canada. These tariffs act as a tax hike on Michigan families and businesses by raising prices at the grocery store and the gas pump," Gretchen Whitmer, the Democratic governor from Michigan posted on social media.

"Michiganders literally cannot afford to keep paying these Republican tariff taxes."

-- With files from Kelly Geraldine Malone

news.title: Father of sailor aboard the beleaguered USS Abraham Lincoln detained by immigration authorities, family says
news.text: The immigrant father of a sailor on board the beleaguered USS Abraham Lincoln was detained Saturday by immigration officials, family members said. Luis Manuel Aviles, originally from Nicaragua, was detained shortly after 11 a.m. ET in Key West, Florida, where he lives, stepdaughter Katty Delgado told NBC News on Saturday evening. She said that Aviles has been in the U.S. for roughly 20 years and that she has no knowledge of an arrest history or criminal allegations against him. “He’s doing everything the right way,” she said. The Department of Homeland Security confirmed Sunday that the Border Patrol arrested Aviles during a traffic stop in Key West. The agency said Aviles entered the U.S. illegally at an unknown date and location and would remain in ICE custody pending removal proceedings. “We are simply enforcing the laws passed by Congress. This Administration does not pick and choose which laws to enforce,” a DHS spokesperson said. Delgado said she learned the news from family members, including Aviles’ wife and his son Joshua Aviles, who posted a note about the detention on Facebook. Her stepfather, Delgado said, was arrested near a Publix supermarket as he was headed to a mechanic. Joshua Aviles said on Facebook that he’s on board the aircraft carrier USS Abraham Lincoln, which is on its way back to the U.S. after its prolonged stretch at sea, including its deployment to the Middle East to engage in the war with Iran. “I’ve been deployed for over nine months, out at sea in the Middle East aboard the USS Abraham Lincoln, fighting for a country that has given me everything,” he wrote Saturday. He said that his father is hard-working, giving and humble and that he has a work permit, a Social Security card and a driver’s license. “This is heartbreaking for me,” Joshua Aviles said. “I don’t know how I can mentally continue working 12+ hour days knowing that my dad is somewhere, possibly being treated like a criminal.” Asked to confirm whether Luis Manuel Aviles had a Social Security number, a work permit or pending immigration cases, as his family indicated, DHS told Telemundo, NBCUniversal’s Spanish-language network, that “work authorization or a pending application do NOT confer legal status in the United States.” The Lincoln left its home port of San Diego on Nov. 25, and, with more than eight months since it visited a port in December, it broke the Navy record for time without a port call. Relatives of sailors on board the carrier have described reports of deteriorating conditions and morale. Defense Secretary Pete Hegseth has said claims about the situation on board have been “completely misrepresented.” The Navy said Saturday that the Lincoln has officially left the Middle East en route to the West Coast, a journey that could take a month or more. Joshua Aviles, who told NBC News he has limited internet access, wrote on Facebook that he’s doing everything he can to get his father released from detention. “I love you with all my heart. Please stay strong. I’m coming home, Dad,” he wrote. President Donald Trump has stood by his administration’s immigration crackdown, including ICE’s expanded enforcement and arrests, which in recent months have included the arrests of children and spouses of service members, a San Diego Padres minor-league catching coordinator and a grandmother from India who’s a schoolteacher with a green card. Immigration authorities have detained more than 50 parents and spouses of service members during Trump’s second term, according to a recent Associated Press investigation. There has been backlash to the detentions, which come despite programs for military members that can sometimes offer immediate family protection from deportation. The U.S. Citizenship and Immigration Services website says those “discretionary options” are offered on a “case-by-case basis.” It was not immediately clear whether Luis Manuel Aviles was in the program. The DHS spokesperson said in a statement Sunday that “having a family member in the military is not a free pass to violate our nation’s laws.” “Military service by an immediate relative does not automatically grant parole, lawful status, or immunity from immigration enforcement,” the spokesperson said. Delgado lamented that her stepbrother has spent nine months out at sea, without seeing his family, “and this is what his father gets.”
news.author: Bill Feather,Dennis Romero

news.title: Trump to visit Ireland for Irish Open at his Doonbeg golf course
news.text: US President Donald Trump plans to visit Ireland on September 12 and 13 to attend the Irish Open golf tournament at his golf course in Doonbeg, County Clare, according to a White House official. During the trip, he is also expected to join an event with US embassy workers and business officials before attending the tournament at Trump International Golf Links Ireland.The visit again puts the focus on the overlap between Trump’s official travel and properties linked to his family business. His sons have taken over the day-to-day control of the Trump Organisation, but the Ireland trip is the latest example of how presidential travel can also benefit the family’s business interests.The White House official, who was not authorised to speak publicly and spoke on condition of anonymity, said Trump would be in Ireland for the two-day visit in September. The trip comes immediately after Trump is expected to campaign for Republicans ahead of the November elections at the Republican Party’s first national convention before the midterm polls. The event, scheduled in Dallas on September 9 and 10, was Trump’s idea and is aimed at building support through a convention-style gathering similar to those usually held before presidential elections.Trump’s golf properties have continued to feature in his travel and public schedule. His course in Bedminster, New Jersey, hosted a LIV golf tournament in August. Another Trump course at Doral in South Florida is set to host a PGA event, the Cadillac Championship, in March 2028. Trump has also spoken about his course in Turnberry, Scotland, hosting the British Open again. The tournament was last held there in 2009, before Trump bought the resort, though a return continues to face major logistical hurdles.Last summer, Trump spent five days in Scotland, where he played golf at Turnberry and later inaugurated a new Trump golf course in Balmedie, Aberdeenshire. The White House did not describe that visit as a holiday and said it was a working trip. During that visit, Trump also spoke about trade with then British Prime Minister Keir Starmer and European Commission President Ursula von der Leyen.Trump often travels to golf courses he owns in Florida and New Jersey, as well as a course in Virginia just outside Washington, DC. He is not known to take long holidays. In his 2004 book, Think Like a Billionaire, Trump wrote: "Don’t take vacations. What’s the point?"As recently as last summer, Trump had criticised Barack Obama for taking long flights to play golf while serving as president. "They talked about the carbon footprint and then Obama hops onto a 747, Air Force One, and flies to Hawaii to play a round of golf and comes back," Trump said last year.Apart from the Scotland visit, the longest stretch of downtime Trump took last year was a December stay at his Mar-a-Lago club in Florida that extended beyond Christmas. Even that trip included visits by Ukrainian President Volodymyr Zelenskyy and Israeli Prime Minister Benjamin Netanyahu. The Ireland trip was first confirmed by the New York Post.In sum, Trump is set to travel to Ireland next month for events involving US officials and business representatives before attending the Irish Open at his Doonbeg golf course, in a visit that once again places attention on the link between his presidential travel and his family’s business interests.With PTI Inputs- EndsPublished By: India Today Web Desk Published On: Aug 24, 2026 05:50 IST

news.title: Inside Turkey’s military machine: Tanks, drones and regional power
news.text: The growing tensions between Israel and Turkey, which have taken on added significance in recent days amid military activity in Syria, have raised anew a question that has become increasingly relevant for Israel's defense establishment in recent years: How powerful is the Turkish military? The answer begins with striking numbers, but certainly does not end there. Turkey is not merely a major NATO member. It is a regional military power whose influence stretches from the Black and Aegean seas through Syria and Iraq to the Caucasus and North Africa. NATO itself described Turkey ahead of the alliance's summit in Ankara in July as the country with the "alliance's second-largest army," after the United States. Its location between Europe, Asia and the Middle East, as well as its control of the Bosporus and Dardanelles straits, gives that power even greater strategic significance. According to Global Firepower data for 2026, which is based in part on estimates, Turkey has about 481,000 active-duty military personnel, 380,000 reservists and another 150,000 members of paramilitary forces. Combined, the three categories account for more than 1 million people. By the number of active-duty personnel, Turkey ranks 10th worldwide according to the index. More than 2,280 tanks and nearly 100,000 vehicles The ground force is the backbone of the Turkish military. According to Global Firepower, its arsenal includes about 2,284 tanks and roughly 98,000 vehicles of various types. Alongside them, Turkey maintains a large artillery force: more than 1,000 self-propelled artillery systems, 635 towed guns and 237 multiple rocket launchers. The figures represent estimated inventories and not necessarily the number of systems available for operational use at any given time. Turkey's equipment is a mix of older Western systems and newer generations of domestically produced platforms. For decades, Ankara relied heavily on American and European weapons, but in recent years it has invested enormous sums in an effort to reduce that dependence, from tanks and armored vehicles to missiles, air defense systems, military electronics and unmanned systems. The result is a military that seeks not only to be large but also to be capable of maintaining and upgrading a growing share of its systems on its own. More than 1,100 aircraft and the F-35 dream According to Global Firepower estimates, the Turkish military has about 1,101 aircraft. The figure includes 201 fighter aircraft, 84 transport planes, 301 training aircraft and 509 helicopters, including 111 attack helicopters. Here, too, the figure represents the total inventory and not necessarily actual operational readiness. The site estimates, for example, that about 141 of the 201 fighter aircraft would be available under its assumed readiness scenario. The backbone of Turkey's fighter fleet remains its F-16s, but Ankara is pursuing two tracks simultaneously: an effort to rejoin the American F-35 fighter jet program, from which it was removed following its purchase of the Russian S-400 system, and the development of its own indigenous fighter jet, the KAAN. The KAAN made its first flight in 2024 and is one of the Turkish defense industry's flagship projects. Ankara sees it as a key component of its plan to reduce dependence on foreign fighter aircraft, although the domestic project still relies on American components, most notably General Electric engines. At the same time, Turkey continues to press Washington to return to the F-35 program. U.S. President Donald Trump expressed openness at the NATO summit in Ankara to allowing the sale of the aircraft to Turkey, but the path remains fraught with legal and political obstacles, including over the S-400 issue. Israel strongly opposes the move out of concern that it could undermine its qualitative military edge in the region, and Prime Minister Benjamin Netanyahu has publicly voiced his opposition. The force that changed the battlefield: Drones If there is one field in which Turkey has quickly become a global name, it is unmanned aerial vehicles. Turkish company Baykar, the manufacturer of the Bayraktar family, turned the TB2 into one of the world's best-known drones following its use in a series of conflicts and later developed more advanced systems, including the TB3. Turkish drones have become not only an operational tool but also an export engine and a diplomatic asset. Turkey markets its systems to dozens of countries and has emerged in this field as a significant competitor to Israeli defense industries in the global market. According to Reuters, Turkish defense industry exports reached about $10 billion in 2025, triple the 2021 figure, and Ankara is now seeking further expansion in European and global markets. 17 frigates, 14 submarines and a ship turned drone carrier The sea is also a central component of Turkey's power projection strategy. According to Global Firepower, the navy has 192 vessels, including 17 frigates, nine corvettes and 14 submarines. Turkey operates its naval forces across three main theaters — the Black Sea, Aegean Sea and Mediterranean — and its location allows it to control the only maritime passage between the Black Sea and the Mediterranean. One of the navy's most prominent platforms is the TCG Anadolu, a multipurpose amphibious assault ship and the largest vessel in the Turkish fleet. After Turkey was removed from the F-35 program, it developed, among other things, a concept under which the ship could serve as a naval base for operating unmanned aircraft. During the EFES-2026 exercise held in May, a Bayraktar TB3 was operated from the ship as part of a combat scenario. Earlier, during a NATO exercise in the Baltic Sea, a TB3 took off autonomously from Anadolu's short deck and struck maritime targets. Through this, Turkey is seeking to develop a relatively new model of naval power: a large ship that extends its operational reach through an array of armed drones. 4,500 companies and more than 1,400 projects One of the deepest changes in Turkey's balance of power is not in the number of soldiers or tanks but in the factories behind them. For years, Turkey was a major customer for foreign weapons systems. Today, it is seeking to become a manufacturer and exporter in its own right. According to data published this month by Anadolu Agency, more than 4,500 companies now operate in Turkey's defense industry, compared with just 56 in 2002, while the number of defense projects has surpassed 1,400. According to the same data, the share of locally produced components and systems has risen from about 20% two decades ago to more than 85% today. The strategic significance is substantial: Turkey is able to produce at home an increasing share of the drones, missiles, armored vehicles, warships and electronic systems it uses while also generating revenue and political influence through their export. And how much does it spend on defense? Turkish defense spending has been rising sharply, although the scale varies considerably depending on the definition and source. In a NATO report on 2025 defense spending, Turkey's expenditure was estimated at about $32.6 billion at that year's prices and exchange rates, up from about $28.3 billion in 2024. NATO estimated that spending amounted to about 2.33% of GDP. The figures for 2024 and 2025 were identified in the report as estimates. Other estimates put Turkey's defense budget higher. Global Firepower, for example, estimates 2026 spending at about $51.4 billion. The discrepancy is due in part to differences in definitions, budget years and calculation methods, meaning comparisons between sources should be made cautiously. Mass, geography, experience and industry So what makes the Turkish military particularly powerful? First and foremost, mass. Hundreds of thousands of soldiers, hundreds of thousands of reservists, thousands of armored vehicles and the ability to mobilize manpower on a scale that few countries in the region can approach. The second advantage is geography: Turkey sits at the intersection of Europe, Asia and the Middle East and controls the Bosporus and Dardanelles straits. It borders, among others, Syria, Iraq, Iran, Georgia and Bulgaria and lies within close reach of the Caucasus, Balkans and eastern Mediterranean. The third advantage is operational experience. The Turkish military has spent years fighting the Kurdistan Workers' Party, carried out a series of operations beyond the country's borders, maintains forces and conducts operations in northern Syria and Iraq and has been involved, directly or indirectly, in additional theaters. The fourth is the defense industry. Unlike a large military that is entirely dependent on external supplies, Turkey is now able to produce an increasing share of its own weapons systems. That does not eliminate its dependence on foreign technology in certain areas, but it gives Ankara significantly greater freedom of action than it had in the past. The fifth advantage is NATO. Turkey has been a member of the alliance since 1952, hosts NATO Allied Land Command in Izmir and is a key component of the alliance's southern flank. Membership provides it with joint training, common military standards, intelligence sharing and cooperation with some of the world's most advanced militaries. Still, numbers alone can be misleading. The Turkish military has equipment from different generations, some of it old, and not every tank, aircraft or vessel listed in its inventory is fully operational. In modern warfare, the question is not simply how many platforms exist, but how many are available, how well protected they are, what intelligence is available to them and how effectively they can operate together on a single network with the air force, navy, drones, artillery and air defense systems. But even with that caveat, the picture is clear: Turkey in 2026 is much more than a "large military." It is a regional military power with enormous manpower, thousands of combat platforms, significant air and naval forces, global leadership in drones and a rapidly growing defense industry. As relations with Israel grow more strained and Turkish influence in Syria expands, that power is becoming for Jerusalem less of a theoretical statistic and more of a strategic consideration that is increasingly difficult to ignore.
news.summary: With 481,000 active-duty troops, more than 2,280 tanks, 1,100 aircraft and nearly 200 naval vessels, Turkey has built a formidable military force, backed by a booming defense industry and a growing arsenal of homegrown weapons

news.title: "Entering the endgame": US Treasury Secy Bessent says "economic D-Day" begins against Iran
news.text:
Washington DC [US], August 24 (ANI): US Treasury Secretary Scott Bessent on Sunday (local time) said that the Trump administration is entering the "endgame" in its campaign against Iran, announcing what he called an "economic D-Day" aimed at severing Iran's economic lifelines.In a post on X, Bessent said, "President Trump has dismantled Iran's military capabilities, destroyed nearly 100 percent of its military factories, and buried its nuclear program."

President Trump has dismantled Iran’s military capabilities, destroyed nearly 100 percent of its military factories, and buried its nuclear program.We are now entering the endgame. At dawn begins an economic D-Day — the single greatest financial offensive ever marshaled against…— Treasury Secretary Scott Bessent (@SecScottBessent) August 23, 2026

"We are now entering the endgame. At dawn begins an economic D-Day -- the single greatest financial offensive ever marshaled against an adversary," he said.Bessent accused Iran of using security guarantees as a form of "extortion" and said Tehran had relied on the expectation that Iranian retaliation was certain while US enforcement could be negotiated."The Islamic Republic has subsisted by dressing extortion as security guarantees. It has drawn strength from a calculus that regards Iranian retaliation as certain and American enforcement as negotiable," Bessent said."Under President Trump, that era is over. And those who fear the danger of defying Tehran ought not to discount the cost of testing Washington," he added.Bessent said Trump had created the conditions for the US government to deploy its full range of authorities against Iran."The President has created the conditions to leverage every agency, every authority and action many assumed we would never summon," he said."Our objective is to sever every economic lifeline that sustains the tyrannical regime until Tehran stands alone," Bessent added.Meanwhile, Iran's Supreme National Security Council Secretary Mohsen Rezaei on Monday warned that Tehran could halt all oil exports through the Strait of Hormuz and elsewhere in the Persian Gulf if the United States' "economic war" against Iran continues.Rezaei, in a post on X, also warned that Iran would consider any country supporting or participating in the US economic campaign against Tehran to be an "act of war.""If the economic war continues, not a single drop of oil will be exported. neither through the Strait of Hormuz nor from anywhere in the Persian Gulf. Iran will regard any country's participation in or support for America's economic war against the Iranian people as an act of war," Rezaei said.The warning comes amid heightened tensions between Tehran and Washington over US plans for tougher economic measures against Iran.Earlier on Sunday, Iranian Parliament Speaker Mohammad Bagher Ghalibaf ridiculed the United States following the fresh economic sanctions threat by President Donald Trump, using satirical commentary to argue that heavy-handed economic restrictions ultimately backfire.In a post on X, Ghalibaf commented on the limitations of trying to manage deep-seated financial strain through short-term state interventions and shared a sarcastic take on how economic pressures play out."Importing frozen meat to fix meat prices. Okay, that might work. What's the plan for bonds, import frozen yields? Frozen homebuyers for housing? Frozen paychecks for wages? A frozen foreign policy delivers a frozen economy. The only thing still moving? The Iran boomerang," he said.Meanwhile, according to Al Jazeera, Iranian Foreign Ministry spokesperson Esmaeil Baghaei also slammed US' sanctions threat and said that war and sanctions are "not unfamiliar" to Iran.He noted that the Islamic Republic has been under sanctions for 20 years. Iran's rebuttal came after Trump on Wednesday announced what he called an "Economic D-Day" campaign against Iran, describing it as the "most crushing economic operation ever taken against any country."Trump said the campaign would amount to "Economic Warfare and Isolation on an unprecedented scale" and called on US allies to join Washington in isolating Iran.Trump also said Washington had "very draconian sanctions" available against Iran and indicated that additional measures could be announced."We have things that we could sanction. We have very draconian sanctions, and we'll see what happens," Trump said while addressing technology leaders.He said Washington would determine its next course of action based on developments, adding that the situation could either result in a significant fall in oil prices or lead to a continuation of the existing measures.On Thursday (local time), US Treasury Secretary Scott Bessent also warned Iran of the "toughest sanctions in history", saying Washington will pursue coordinated economic isolation against Tehran and seek to "collapse this regime", Al Jazeera reported.He urged US allies to join Washington in isolating Tehran, claiming that the measures would weaken Iran's ability to project influence globally.Bessent added that a media conference on Monday, i.e August 24, would reveal "exactly what we're going to do" against Iran. (ANI)

news.text: President Donald Trump laughed off the multiple assassination attempts against him, remarking that "only consequential presidents get shot" during an interview with his former personal lawyer Michael Cohen on Sunday. Cohen released the second part of his two-part interview with Trump in which the two dived into additional topics, such as reports that Trump secretly boarded a separate military jet in response to a credible Iranian threat against his life. The former Trump critic pointed out that this was only the latest in a series of attempts on the president's life. "I'm so nauseated by them," Cohen said. "There is a huge difference between vehemently disagreeing with a policy and then trying to literally assassinate the President of the United States." TRUMP'S DECADE OF ASSASSINATION THREATS RUNS FROM BUTLER SHOOTING TO LATEST GOLF CLUB BREACH "The one thing I would say to that. If you read, only consequential presidents get shot," Trump quipped. "Then do me a favor, please don't be consequential. How's that?" Cohen said. "I know. Maybe I'll have to become less consequential," Trump responded. Trump acknowledged that he has a "dangerous" job but added that he has "great people" looking after him. I SERVED AS TRUMP’S NSA. SCOTUS NEED TO STOP COURTS PUTTING THE PRESIDENT'S SECURITY AT RISK "Obviously, it's gotten much, much tougher over the years. But it is true, consequential. You look at the people that were shot. You look at the people, even the attempts, but non-consequential presidents lead a much nicer life. You can see that with some of our recent presidents where nothing was ever even thought about," Trump said. Cohen was originally a key witness in two New York cases against Trump and a frequent critic of the president prior to his interview on Thursday. In a Substack post he penned detailing the stunning reunion that was their first public conversation in nearly a decade, Cohen emphasized the importance of forgiveness despite the backlash he faced for the interview. Forgive as the Lord forgave you,’" he wrote. "That verse isn’t merely some theological footnote to what is happening between Donald Trump and me. It is the foundation of it." news.title: Hasan Piker Sang About Charlie Kirk. The Crowd Cheered. That Says Plenty.
news.text:
Most Americans are pretty good at leaving each other alone. Vote differently, worship differently, live differently, and go home to your family. But there are lines decent people recognize without needing a political consultant to explain them. Hurt children, brutalize women, or torment a grieving family.

Hasan sings “We Are Charlie Kirk” at the Fear& live tour pic.twitter.com/n4rGVTREyB— yeet (@Awk20000) August 22, 2026

Something basic in us recoils.

Hasan Piker found one of those lines Friday night in San Francisco and danced on it.

During a live performance of his Fears& podcast, Piker led a packed theater in a mocking rendition of "We Are Charlie Kirk," a tribute song that appeared after Charlie Kirk was assassinated at Utah Valley University last Sept. 10.

His co-hosts laughed, the audience cheered and sang along, and Piker later posted a photo from the show with the caption, "Carried the flame tn."

Jonathan Turley says what many of us are thinking:

What is exasperating is how hatemongers on the left want to enjoy hate speech while accusing others of hate and intolerance. They do so by excusing their actions or views by demonizing those who disagree. Democratic leaders continue the false claim that democracy is dying in America and that this may be our last free election. While made over multiple elections, the claim of the imminent death of democracy (unless they are elected) does not appear to register with their supporters.Recently the rhetoric has reached hysterical levels. Florida Democratic Senate candidate Angie Nixon has compared Immigration and Customs Enforcement agents to “modern-day slave catchers” and the government is “literally trying to kill us.”It is a narrative that allows you to speak like a Nazi while claiming to be fighting Nazis.Piker thrilled the crowd by mocking a murdered man over his faith and his death. It is more than being simply classless. It is commodifying rage. Piker is reportedly raking in a fortune as are other hatemongers like Jennifer Welch. They traffic in rage to a nation of rage addicts.It is a scene that only reaffirms the work of Kirk who sought to expose the hate and intolerance of the left, particularly on our campuses. Kirk infuriated many by challenging them to debate. There is no room for reason in an age of rage. Those who try to introduce opposing views on campuses are cancelled or attacked.

The timing makes the performance even uglier. Turning Point USA is preparing to return to Utah Valley University on Sept. 10 for a memorial marking one year since Kirk was murdered there. 

From Newsmax:

The conservative youth organization said the "Freedom Built to Last" gathering will remember Kirk as a Christian husband and father, a free-speech advocate, and a leader who helped build a movement among young Americans."The gathering will honor Charlie as a faith-filled husband, father, and defender of free speech," Turning Point said in Friday's release, calling the event "a deliberate act of remembrance, and a call for students and supporters to continue his life's work."The memorial will be held at UVU's UCCU Center, about a five-minute walk from the amphitheater where Kirk was fatally shot while speaking to thousands of students during the opening stop of his "All-American Comeback Tour."Speakers will include conservative talk-show host and Blaze Media founder Glenn Beck; Christian author Frank Turek, a friend and mentor to Kirk; and Turning Point Chief Field Officer Andrew Sypher.

Erika Kirk, Charlie's widow and now CEO and board chair of Turning Point USA, will help lead an organization and a family into an anniversary nobody should ever have to mark.

Piker knew what he was mocking, and so did the crowd.

From Legal Insurrection:

The backlash from conservatives intensified as video of Piker’s disturbing display ricocheted across the internet Saturday.Appalled by Piker’s deliberate mockery of the man who had once been his close friend and mentor, Turning Point spokesman Andrew Kolvet wrote, “Hasan Piker is engaging in pure, unadulterated evil. ‘Whoever gloats over disaster will not go unpunished.’ Proverbs 17:5”Conservative firebrand Jack Posobiec noted in the X post below, “Here is Hasan Piker now mocking the murder of Charlie Kirk as we approach the 1 year anniversary of his assassination. The Bolsheviks will kill us all and they will laugh about it.”Responding to Posobiec, Rep. Brandon Gill (R-TX) wrote, “These aren’t just people who disagree with us politically. They are enemies of everything that is good and holy about our civilization. And they will stop at nothing to destroy it.

His political record deserves attention because he's no longer merely an internet provocateur shouting into a camera. Piker has said Hamas is "1,000 times better" than Israel, said he had no issues with Hezbollah, compared liberal Zionists to "liberal Nazis," and previously apologized for calling ultra-Orthodox Jews "inbred."

Piker rejected accusations that he's antisemitic and says he opposes anti-Jewish violence. His own words still leave a remarkable record for others to judge.

Michigan Democratic Sen. nominee Abdulrahman Mohamed El-Sayed chose to campaign with Piker at Michigan State University and the University of Michigan in April. El-Sayed defended the appearance as a way to reach young people who feel shut out of politics. 

He later won Michigan's Democrat Senate primary, becoming one of the most prominent progressive nominees of 2026.

Democratic Socialists of America (DSA) hasn't swallowed the Democrat Party.

Very few Democrat candidates are members. Its growing influence, however, is becoming hard to dismiss. The organization says it has more than 100,000 members and has endorsed 150 candidates this year. Democratic Sen. Chris Van Hollen of Maryland said Sunday that the DSA deserves a place in the debate over his party's return.

The country remains far less enthusiastic. A July poll found only 27% of Americans believe democratic socialists have at least some good ideas, while 51% say they have few or none.

So Democrats eventually have to answer a difficult question. After a decade in which opposition to President Donald Trump became one of the party's defining forces, what else has been allowed through the door?

Political movements reveal themselves partly through what they celebrate, tolerate, and refuse to condemn. The first anniversary of his murder is approaching. His widow, family, friends, and organization are preparing to remember him.

Hasan Piker gave his crowd a song while they gave him cheers.

Character sometimes announces itself very clearly.

news.title: Pezeshkian Says Iran Faces Mounting Economic Strains
news.text:
Pezeshkian, speaking in a televised address, said his government recognized the pressures facing Iranian society and was working to prevent conditions from deteriorating further.



"I understand that our society is currently facing several difficulties,” Pezeshkian said. "We are doing everything we can to prevent the situation from worsening.”



His remarks came as Washington prepared additional economic measures targeting Iran, nearly six months after U.S. and Israeli strikes in late February triggered a wider conflict. U.S. officials have said the sanctions campaign is intended to further isolate Iran economically and increase pressure on its leadership.



Pezeshkian described the confrontation as extending beyond financial restrictions. "We are facing an all-out war on the economic, military and security fronts,” he said, referring to U.S. President Donald Trump’s statements about imposing what the Iranian leader characterized as the most severe sanctions against his country.



The pressure is increasingly visible across Iran’s economy. Inflation, unemployment, currency weakness and higher living costs have strained household finances, with food prices and essential expenses taking a larger share of family incomes. Disruptions linked to the conflict have also complicated transportation and commercial activity.



Recent reporting from inside Iran has documented households reducing purchases as prices rise, adding a civilian dimension to the economic concerns acknowledged by Pezeshkian. 



"We are striving to overcome inflation, livelihood problems and unemployment and to secure the future of the people so they can live with dignity and pride,” Pezeshkian said.



Iranian Foreign Minister Abbas Araghchi has rejected Washington’s threatened sanctions, describing the U.S. approach as an act of desperation and arguing that additional economic pressure will not force Tehran to abandon its position. His remarks illustrate the competing approaches confronting Iran: maintaining resistance to U.S. demands while managing mounting domestic economic pressures.



Economic grievances have previously developed into wider political unrest. Demonstrations that began in late December over soaring living costs spread across the country and expanded into protests against Iran’s leadership.



Iranian authorities have reported more than 3,000 deaths during the unrest and attributed much of the violence to what they called "terrorist acts,” accusing the United States and Israel of involvement. Rights organizations operating outside Iran have reported thousands of deaths and accused Iranian security forces of using deadly force against demonstrators.



According to observers, Pezeshkian’s acknowledgment of economic hardship highlights the domestic stakes of Iran’s confrontation with Washington. Further sanctions could intensify pressure on trade, employment and household purchasing power, leaving Tehran to balance economic stability and public expectations with its continuing security and diplomatic confrontation with the United States.

news.title: Iran rips Trump's 'empty talk' while issuing blistering ultimatum to neighboring nations
news.text:
Iran has dismissed Donald Trump's threats of economic warfare as 'empty talk' while warning neighboring countries not to help Washington squeeze Tehran.

Iran's powerful security chief Mohsen Rezaei threatened retaliation against any nearby nation that joins the US crackdown and warned Tehran could stop oil from flowing through the Persian Gulf.

'If countries neighboring Iran cooperate with the Americans in the economic war, we will target their interests,' Rezaei declared.

'The world has realized that Trump's bluster is nothing but empty talk,' Rezaei said in an interview with Iranian state media on Saturday.

He then turned his fire on countries surrounding Iran, warning that Tehran could dramatically widen its economic confrontation if they side with Washington.

Iran does not want to expand the war across the Middle East, Rezaei insisted, but he delivered a threat to his neighbors.

'If they start such an action, we will not allow a single drop of oil to pass through the Persian Gulf,' Rezaei added.

The warning potentially puts major Gulf energy producers on notice as Trump prepares to ratchet up his campaign of economic pressure against Tehran.

Saudi Arabia and the United Arab Emirates have spent years developing and expanding alternative export routes that reduce their reliance on the Strait of Hormuz, allowing oil to reach ports on the Red Sea and Gulf of Oman.

But Rezaei indicated those routes may not necessarily be beyond Tehran's reach either, threatening alternative pathways used to move Gulf oil to international markets.

His comments amount to one of the clearest warnings yet that Iran's hardline security establishment could increasingly regard cooperation with Washington's economic campaign as participation in the wider conflict.

Rezaei also insisted that Iran would 'neutralize the economic war' being waged by the US, with the Trump administration expected to unveil details of tougher sanctions on Monday.

The combative rhetoric comes amid growing indications of a potentially serious split at the highest levels of power in Tehran.

While Rezaei is promising resistance and threatening retaliation, Iranian President Masoud Pezeshkian struck a dramatically different tone on Sunday, declaring that his country 'cannot continue with war forever.'

Pezeshkian openly defended the memorandum of understanding Iran reached with the United States in June, despite reported reservations from Supreme Leader Mojtaba Khamenei.

That agreement ultimately collapsed last month.

But the Iranian president argued that Tehran cannot remain indefinitely trapped between outright conflict and an elusive peace.

'One day, a decision must be made to save the country from the state of "neither war nor peace,"' Pezeshkian said.

He maintained that officials directly involved in negotiations believed the agreement with Washington had offered Iran its best available path forward.

'By implementing this memorandum, we can resolve the problems with logic and dignity,' Pezeshkian said, according to Iranian state news agency IRNA.

Pezeshkian made clear Sunday that military strength alone could not protect the Islamic Republic if its people lost faith in their government.

'We must stand with the people,' he said. 'If we cannot serve them and convince them that we all belong to the same land and country, then even if we possess the greatest military power, we will be defeated.'

The president said his government was fighting to improve the lives of Iranians battered by the country's economic difficulties.

It was trying with all its strength, he said, to 'steer inflation, public problems, people's livelihoods, people's jobs, people's future, and people's lives towards dignity and pride.'

'Sometimes, a wise compromise can achieve more than hundreds of wars,' Khomeini said.

But Rezaei's comments suggest Iran's powerful military-security establishment is preparing for precisely the opposite possibility.

The former senior military commander said Iran would introduce new capabilities and alter its approach across several fronts.

'We will see changes in the conduct of the war, in diplomacy, and in political and social affairs, and new capabilities will be brought into play,' he said.

Rezaei, an adviser to Supreme Leader Khamenei, also declared that Tehran would refuse to bow to US demands and maintained that the Strait of Hormuz would remain closed until Washington fulfilled what Iran considers its commitments.

The strait has become one of Tehran's most powerful weapons in its showdown with Washington because of its enormous importance to the global energy trade.

But there are signs that Iran's ability to exert pressure through the waterway could be challenged.

Shipping data indicates more crude is now leaving the Gulf using a southern route close to Oman, while some oil companies have developed tactics designed to allow tankers to make the journey without being detected.

That threatens to erode some of the leverage Tehran has exercised by restricting one of the world's most strategically important energy corridors.
news.summary: Iran dismissed Donald Trump's threats as 'empty talk' as Washington prepares to ramp up economic pressure on Tehran.

news.title: Morocco’s attempt to rebrand Western Sahara
news.text:
The city of Dakhla, on a “peninsula where the Sahara meets the Atlantic”, is advertised to holidaymakers as “Morocco’s hidden gem”, said the BBC. But tourists flying to this part of Western Sahara might not know they’ll “be landing in one of the world’s longest ongoing territorial disputes”.

A former Spanish colony, Western Sahara was annexed by Morocco in 1975. Since then, it has been the subject of a dispute between Morocco and its indigenous Sahrawi people, led by the Polisario Front and its government-in-exile in Algeria. Now classified by the United Nations as a “non-self-governing territory”, around 80% of the country is occupied and administered by Morocco, with an earthen strip separating that area from a Sahrawi-controlled portion in the east. Numerous UN-brokered talks to resolve Western Sahara’s future have failed.

‘Tomorrow’s Dubai’

Morocco has been pouring considerable resources into Western Sahara. Since 2015, it has spent £7 billion trying to “level it up”, said The Spectator. There are now water desalination plants, 620 miles of motorways, and plans for eight “green hydrogen plants” and a “centrepiece” £1 billion Dakhla Atlantic Port. This “massive undertaking” is still under construction but, when finished, “35 million tons of goods are expected to pass through every year”.

King Mohammed VI’s “development plan” for the country he refers to as Morocco’s “Southern Provinces” includes “metamorphosing” Western Sahara’s coastline into a hub for business and tourism. Christopher Nolan filmed several scenes for “The Odyssey” on the “otherworldly” White Dune, just outside Dakhla, and it’s hoped many will want “to follow Odysseus’ footsteps and flock” to this city on the up: “think of it as tomorrow’s Dubai”.

Western Sahara also has plenty of natural resources that Morocco could exploit. Surveys have pointed to “promising deposits for gold, silver and iron” in the region, said Bloomberg.

‘International consensus’ shift

Nolan’s decision to film in Western Sahara was bound to “revive debate” over this “half-century-old territorial dispute”, said Bloomberg. Morocco’s annexation has created “one of the world’s most enduring yet overlooked refugee crises”, said Metro. For the past 50 years, the indigenous Sahrawi people have been “forced to live under occupation or go into exile”: 173,000 Sahrawi refugees live in camps in Algeria, in the “harshest part of the desert”. Each camp is named after a city in Western Sahara, but “many have never set foot” in these places “where their parents or grandparents were born”.

In recent years, international consensus has shifted and consolidated in favour of Morocco’s “autonomy plan” for Western Sahara. Spain has endorsed the plan and both France and the US have recognised Morocco’s sovereignty over the region. In October, the UN Security Council approved a resolution that gave the “strongest backing yet” to Moroccan control, “while making no mention of the independence referendum” sought by the Polisaro Front, said Bloomberg.

Last month, Donald Trump thanked Moroccan authorities for naming a highway after him, said Al Jazeera. The gesture has not been confirmed by Rabat but “would be far from surprising”, since the US has provided “crucial support” in bringing Morocco “closer to securing greater control” over the Western Sahara. In recent weeks, the US Department of Commerce announced it would fund “the early stages of an ammonium project” in the region, adding “a new economic dimension” to the long-running, “competing claims over the territory”.
news.summary: Rabat investing billions in territory, despite ongoing dispute over autonomy and control

news.title: Iran to consider any participation in US economic operation ‘act of war,’ says security official
news.text:
Tehran, Aug 24 (SocialNews.XYZ) A senior Iranian security official warned that the country will consider any state's participation in or support for the US anti-Iran economic operation as an "act of war."

In a social media post, Mohsen Rezaei, secretary of Iran's Supreme National Security Council, said, "If the economic war continues, not a single drop of oil will be exported, neither through the Strait of Hormuz nor from anywhere in the Persian Gulf. Iran will regard any country's participation in or support for America's economic war against the Iranian people as an act of war."

His remarks came in response to recent comments made by US President Donald Trump, reports Xinhua news agency.

In a Wednesday post on Truth Social, Trump announced "the most crushing economic operation ever taken" against any country providing a lifeline to Iran.

"This will be Economic Warfare and Isolation on an unprecedented scale," he said, calling the move "an ECONOMIC D-DAY."

Earlier, Rezaei warned that any country participating in the US economic war against Iran will be considered an "enemy" by Tehran.

Rezaei, the secretary of Iran's Supreme National Security Council, made the remarks on Saturday in an interview with state-run IRIB TV.

He said Iran would first negotiate with such countries and ask them to stay out of the conflict, but warned that if they refuse, Tehran will strike their interests, and that if surrounding countries choose to join the US siege, Iran "will not let even a single drop of oil be exported from the Strait of Hormuz."

He noted that Iran has learned how to bypass US sanctions and continue oil sales over the years, Xinhua news agency reported.

Rezaei also repeated that the Hormuz Strait will remain closed unless the United States fulfills its commitments under the Iran-US peace memorandum of understanding signed in June, adding that Washington must act first this time.

On June 18, the United States and Iran signed a memorandum of understanding (MoU) on ending the war in the region on all fronts, including Lebanon. Under the MoU, they were scheduled to hold negotiations within 60 days, which ended on Monday, to reach a final agreement, but the fate of the talks remains unclear following the escalation between the two countries last month.

news.title: Ukraine backers gather as war escalates, air defence runs low
news.text: Ukraine on Monday hosts a meeting of its key European backers to press for critical air-defence supplies and more pressure on Moscow, with Russian attacks killing more civilians than at any time since the first months of the invasion. The meeting of the Coalition of the Willing will be jointly chaired by the leaders of Britain, France and Germany. UK Prime Minister Andy Burnham will be in Kyiv for his first international trip since entering 10 Downing Street, and several other leaders are expected to join remotely. EU Council President Antonio Costa is also due in Kyiv for the talks, which come amid the latest, deadly escalation of the war. Russia has been pounding Kyiv with ballistic missiles in recent weeks, ripping open apartment blocks and killing dozens of citizens in the capital. The escalating Russian strikes have pushed civilian deaths to their highest levels since the first months of Russia's 2022 invasion. After almost every attack -- which sees tens of thousands hunker in the Kyiv metro system and many more in basements and other shelters across the city -- Zelensky has issued public pleas for more air-defence support. - UK, French support - Ukraine celebrates independence day on Monday, which also marks exactly four-and-a-half years since Russia invaded on February 24, 2022. "Russia should be in no doubt of our resolve," Burnham said in a statement before his arrival in Kyiv. "We will not back down until there is a just and lasting peace." Diplomacy on ending the conflict -- Europe's largest since World War II -- is effectively frozen. Russia is demanding hardline territorial and political concessions that Kyiv has rejected as a capitulation that would only enable another Russian attack. Burnham is set to announce that the British government is authorising defence firm MBDA to release classified information needed to help Ukraine and France set up local production of the long-range SCALP missile. And on Saturday, French President Emmanuel Macron pledged Paris would deliver new interceptor missiles. "It is crucial to provide Ukraine with all the necessary means to defend its skies and thwart this aggression," Macron wrote on X. The ballistic missiles Russia has been firing in their dozens are incredibly fast and travel with a high-arching trajectory, making them difficult to stop. Kyiv's home-grown weapons cannot shoot them down, meaning Ukraine is reliant on advanced systems -- chiefly, US Patriot interceptors -- to protect its skies. But amid shortfalls globally since the US launched its war on Iran, Ukraine has been left exposed. - Ukraine's missiles shortfall - Ahead of the meeting, Zelensky revealed the extent of the deficit, releasing usually closely guarded numbers. He said deliveries of crucial Patriot interceptors had halved since 2023. "Over the entire of 2023, Ukraine received 675 missiles, and over all of 2025 -- 364, even though Russian missile strikes have increased," Zelensky said. "For 2026, as currently projected, it is 264," he added, saying Ukraine was seeking a package of at least 300 for the upcoming winter. The United States faces its own shortfall of the missiles amid its war on Iran and has resisted releasing large numbers to Ukraine. Zelensky said Russia could produce around 100 ballistic missiles a month. Ukraine, meanwhile, has accelerated its own campaign of long-range strikes on Russian energy and logistics sites -- including oil refineries and retail warehouses. The Coalition of the Willing is a Franco-British initiative to deliver support to Ukraine and ramp up pressure on Russia. Originally designed as a group of countries that would be willing to deploy peacekeeping troops to Ukraine in the event a ceasefire was reached, it has become a parallel forum for marshalling support to Ukraine amid uncertainty over US commitments under Donald Trump. bur-jc/jj/hol

news.title: Marco Rubio and the Trump Administration Champion Western Civilization
news.text:
In the Trump era of tariffs, chastisement, and charged rhetoric, one could be forgiven for thinking that relations between America and Europe are currently at a low ebb.

Over the course of his two administrations, President Donald Trump has imposed tariffs on European goods, upbraided NATO allies for not paying their fair share of military costs, and, for a beat or two, refused to rule out the use of force to acquire Greenland, a territory of the Kingdom of Denmark, before later walking back what these remarks seemed to intimate.

While the Trump administration has at times taken a hard policy and rhetorical line in its relations with the EU and European governments, its attitude toward European civilization has been consistent and hopeful.

In a speech at the most important security conference in the world in Munich in February, Marco Rubio, America’s chief diplomat, did not wave a finger at his European hosts. Instead, he chose to stress the shared history, culture, friendship, and destiny of Europe and the United States.

As a pithy rehearsal of what counts as “Western civilization,” Rubio’s short speech was a masterclass. The very fact that he used the term “Western civilization” repeatedly and unapologetically was itself a breath of fresh air, especially for those of us who may remember President Barack Obama’s run of speeches in Europe, dubbed “an apology tour” by critics.

Rubio did not shy away from cheering Western cultural achievements, of which he spoke in almost religious terms. The inheritance of the West was “sacred,” he declared, rooted in a shared history, faith, culture, heritage, language, and ancestry.

What does any of this have to do with security?

Rubio’s answer was precise and used to count as so much common sense. Armies do not fight for abstract international organizations, but for their countries. They defend borders, a shared culture, and the brother next to them; they fight, not for the end of history, but for liberty and the hope of a prosperous future for their children.

The late philosopher Roger Scruton coined a term that summarizes this idea nicely: oikophilia, or love of home. Scruton also talked in terms of “the sacred” when attempting to describe what we love most about the place we call home.

A home, Scruton argues, is something loved because it is ours, a place that is open to friends, yes, but also with doors closed to the uninvited. Sacred precincts are polluted when trespassed by those not welcome, the kind of profanation that makes the familiar feel alien and no longer like the home we once knew and loved.

Flight from our shared past, culture, and faith is precisely what Rubio says America under President Trump wishes to arrest, the kind of stand the West has made so many times before at moments of great crisis. Rubio stressed the shared victories of Europe and America through two hot wars and one cold war, and moments of existential import like the Cuban Missile Crisis and the erection of the Berlin Wall.

While it is important to remember what the West should oppose, the Secretary of State reminded us that is far more important to remember why. Yes, the West ought to oppose communism, the “climate cult,” mass immigration, and so forth. Yes, the West has, at times, undermined its own principles and ought to hold itself to account.

But lasting civilizations are not merely reactionary, nor do they wallow.

The greatest traditions laud the achievements of their ancestors and work to hand them on to generations to come. This is literally what the word tradition means: to hand on. Civilization is the fruit of the vine and the work of many hands.

Ours is the civilization that produced Shakespeare, Mozart, Beethoven, and Dante. It was quite moving to hear Rubio rattle off the names of such giants and proudly, too.

Rubio is right to use language that borders on the religious to sum all of this up. The achievements of Western civilization, of which America has been the foremost champion in the modern world, ought to be regarded as sacrosanct. Our civilization is something irreplaceable and unique. Like a person we love, another will not do just as well. Leah cannot stand in for Rachel.

For believers in Western civilization, it is heartening to hear from a man who holds one of the highest offices in the land and understands that we fight hardest for what we love most. To paraphrase another great believer in the West, J.R.R Tolkien, we love the sword not for what it does, but for what it defends: our home.

news.title: Trump is heading to his golf course in Ireland in September
news.text:
WASHINGTON (AP) — President Donald Trump plans to visit Ireland next month to attend the Irish Open golf tournament at his golf course in Doonbeg in County Clare on the country’s Atlantic coast, according to a White House official.

The trip is the most recent example of how the president blurs the line between official business and travel in ways that can benefit his family business. His sons have taken over day-to-day control of the Trump Organization, but the September trip once again lays bare how Trump has leveraged his second term to pad his family’s profits in a variety of ways. 

Trump is scheduled to be in Ireland on Sept. 12 and 13 and will join an event with U.S. embassy workers and business officials before attending the golf tournament at Trump International Golf Links Ireland in Doonbeg, according to the White House official, who was not authorized to speak publicly and spoke on condition of anonymity.

Trump’s course in Bedminster, New Jersey, hosted a LIV golf tournament in August. Another Trump course at Doral in South Florida is scheduled to host a PGA event, the Cadillac Championship, in March 2028, and Trump has talked about his course in Turnberry, Scotland, hosting the British Open, which it last did in 2009, before Trump bought the resort. A return of the British Open to that property continues to face major logistical hurdles. 

Last summer, Trump went to Scotland for five days to golf at Turnberry and later inaugurated a new Trump golf course in Balmedie, Aberdeenshire.
